content:
Three weeks before Election Day, Webb County has a new plan to clean up its voter rolls — and it involves the most sensitive number you own.

Precinct 3 Commissioner John Galo wants county agencies to share data so the elections office can verify identities when striking deceased voters from the rolls, KGNS reported Oct. 13. The missing piece, Galo says, is Social Security numbers: "Now, what we are lacking, and we're going to seek to get permission for, is Social Security numbers."

Here is the current system, and it is barely a system at all. Laredo public health officials compile a monthly list from death certificates — names and addresses only, no Social Security numbers — and hand-deliver it to the county elections office. Paper to hand, in 2026. Galo's argument is that the list cannot tell a dead voter from a living voter with the same name, or flag someone who moved since they last voted. He says the goal is an accurate roll so deceased voters get removed instead of lingering.

What nobody has shown yet

No count. The county has not said how many deceased voters it believes are on the rolls — not one number. A proposal to pipe Social Security numbers between agencies would be a lot easier to judge if anyone had quantified the problem it claims to solve.

No vote, no date. The proposal is still under review, according to KGNS, and county leaders plan to check whether sharing SSNs is even legal before it goes anywhere. There is no vote scheduled.

No privacy plan. Beyond the legal review, nothing has been said publicly about how the numbers would be stored, who could access them, or what audit trail would exist. One resident told KGNS she supports the goal of stopping mistakes before they happen — and that is the entire public debate so far.

No effect on this election. Early voting opened Oct. 19 and runs through Oct. 30. Even if the proposal were approved tomorrow, it could not touch the Nov. 3 rolls.

What Webb Watch is asking

Has the county attorney issued an opinion on whether sharing SSNs is legal? How many dead voters does the county think are on the rolls right now? Which agencies currently hold the Social Security numbers, and how would they be transmitted? Will Commissioners Court hold a public vote? We will keep watching this one — because the moment a county starts trading Social Security numbers, the public deserves more than a hand-delivered list and a promise.

Sources: KGNS (Elena Stoica), Oct. 13, 2026; Webb Watch 956 reporting.

Webb Watch 956
excerpt: A Webb County commissioner wants Social Security numbers shared between agencies to scrub deceased voters from the rolls — with no count of the problem, no vote date, and no privacy plan yet.
title: Dead Voters or Paper Ghosts? Webb County Wants Social Security Numbers to Clean the Rolls
